papers.title: Probabilistic Power Estimation and MPC-based Scheduling of Construction Electric Vehicles Supported by Mobile Charging Stations
papers.abstract: The adoption of construction electric vehicles (CEVs) is held back by sparse on-site charging infrastructure, limited mobility, and insufficient knowledge of their power consumption. Mobile charging stations (MCSs) towed between grid connection points and construction sites address the first barrier, yet scheduling them optimally requires an accurate estimate of the CEV power consumption. In this paper, we address these gaps, first, by estimating the power of each subactivity of a representative CEV (a compact electric excavator) based on real-world construction demonstration data. We use Bayesian linear regression to obtain the subactivity power distributions, accounting for their operational uncertainty. Second, we formulate a mixed-integer program that jointly schedules CEV work and charging together with MCS routing, charging, and discharging, optimizing electricity costs, carbon emissions, work completion, and MCS travel. We embed the optimizer in a shrinking-horizon model predictive control (MPC) loop to perform real-time control on the CEV-MCS system. Two MPC variants, one a certainty-equivalent MPC (CE-MPC) controller, and the other a scenario-based MPC (SB-MPC) controller, are compared in closed-loop against an open-loop day-ahead schedule. Realistic simulations show that SB-MPC performs the best, lowering the operating costs by $60.2\%$ relative to the open-loop baseline, and by $23.3\%$ relative to CE-MPC, demonstrating the efficacy of incorporating predictive control with feedback. The code is available at https://github.com/Shubhanflash22/CEV-MCS-MPC-Joint-Scheduling
papers.reason: MILP scheduling of construction EVs with mobile charging stations under MPC with uncertainty, directly matching electrified fleet scheduling and charging optimisation.

papers.title: Grid-Responsive Pricing of Dynamic Wireless Charging with Coupled Residential Demand
papers.abstract: Dynamic wireless charging (DWC) is an emerging technology that enables electric vehicles (EVs) to recharge while traveling. Its unique operational model creates two revenue streams for DWC operators through lane access tolls and electricity sales. However, these prices influence not only traffic flow and roadway energy delivery but also how much EV charging moves to homes instead, potentially within the same distribution network. Neglecting this coupling can underestimate grid loading and compromise pricing decisions. We develop a coupled traffic, EV energy, driver-response, and AC distribution network model with a model predictive control (MPC) framework that jointly optimizes DWC tolls and charging prices while explicitly accounting for displaced residential charging and network losses. Using 78 days of I-210 West traffic data, we show that conventional MPC exceeds feeder loading limits on 52 days, whereas the proposed residential load aware controller eliminates these violations with only 0.6% lower operator revenue. Under a more constrained feeder configuration, it eliminates 50 overloaded days with a 0.9% revenue reduction. Sensitivity analyses highlight the importance of accurate residential demand estimation and feeder loss modeling, while peak-aware pricing further reduces daily peak loading by 3.7% relative to the base load. These results demonstrate the value of coordinated pricing that captures the interaction between roadway and residential charging.
papers.reason: Jointly prices dynamic wireless charging for EVs with residential charging displacement and feeder loading via MPC; directly on transport-grid integration.

papers.title: Agent-Guided Configuration Tuning for SMT Solvers
papers.abstract: SMT solvers expose many configuration choices that determine how well their existing algorithms perform on a workload. We present, to our knowledge, the first workflow that uses general-purpose LLM agents to tune SMT solver configurations. Agents read solver documentation, source code, and persistent experiment records to propose option changes, and a deterministic harness measures each proposal, validates the returned models, and selects changes separately for each competition Division. Over roughly nine weeks, our tuning campaign recorded 4,545 proposals for cvc5 across 13 Divisions and 36 logics. We evaluate the tuned configurations on the 2026 and 2025 SMT-COMP ModelValidation benchmarks under a 24-second cutoff. On problems not used for training, they validate more problems than official cvc5 in ten of the 13 Divisions in 2026 and in eight in 2025, with geometric-mean gains of 7.8% and 6.8% across Divisions. On the complete official selections, which include training problems, the tuned floating-point counts exceed those of every individual competition participant in both years. Further studies show how configuration changes make existing algorithms effective by changing access to strategies, scheduling, and option compatibility, and how benchmark families trade off against one another. The agents' experiment traces contain hypothesis-based proposals in every tuning group, and 64.3% of the extracted hypotheses draw on prior measurements. These results show that agent-guided tuning can specialize a mature SMT solver and that accumulated experimental evidence informs sustained search.
papers.reason: LLM agents tuning solver configurations with experiment records and a deterministic harness; agents running optimisation pipelines.

papers.title: An Explainable Agentic AI Framework for Distribution System Load Restoration
papers.abstract: Distribution system load restoration is a sequential decision-making problem in which restoration actions must maximize served load, prioritize critical loads, and preserve power-flow feasibility. This paper proposes an explainable agentic artificial intelligence (AI) framework for distribution system load restoration. The proposed framework uses multiple large language model (LLM) agents for planner guidance, strategic plan generation, decision arbitration, memory-based feedback, and explanation generation. Unlike unconstrained LLM-based control, the proposed method restricts agent decisions to feasible restoration actions and evaluates all candidate plans using deterministic AC power-flow feasibility checks. The framework is evaluated on IEEE 33-bus and 69-bus distribution feeders, as well as a larger IEEE 118-bus test case, and compared against reinforcement learning and planning baselines. The results show that the proposed agentic framework achieves better restoration performance while producing structured explanations for operator-facing decision support. A direct comparison with a Single-LLM-Agent baseline further shows that the proposed multi-agent decomposition improves weighted restored load and critical-load recovery compared with a monolithic LLM decision structure.
papers.reason: Multi-LLM agentic framework for distribution system load restoration with AC power-flow checks; operational decisions in power systems, close to grid and agentic interests.

papers.title: Consensus-based Economic Dispatch for Self-organized Local Energy Communities
papers.abstract: The increasing penetration of distributed energy resources (DERs) is transforming traditional distribution networks into dynamic, decentralized systems, creating a pressing need for scalable, autonomous coordination mechanisms that do not rely on centralized control or full system observability. In particular, local energy communities need to self-organize and coordinate energy schedules while respecting network constraints, especially voltage limits, despite lacking detailed knowledge of the distribution grid's topology and parameters. Existing distributed optimization approaches either neglect such physical constraints or assume perfect knowledge of the network model. This paper addresses the Voltage-Constrained Economic Dispatch (VCED) problem in a fully decentralized, consensus-based manner, without any coordinating entity. We use sparse-group LASSO regression to learn a linear surrogate of nodal voltages from local power and voltage measurements alone. The surrogate serves a dual purpose: it enters each agent's local problem as a voltage penalty and induces the communication graph over which the agents reach consensus. We provide a theoretical bound on the optimality loss caused by the surrogate voltage estimator inaccuracy. Our numerical results, on an IEEE-33 network, show that the scheme reduces the share of bus-timesteps voltage violations from 30\% to below 3\%, while staying within 1\% of a centralized benchmark computed with full network knowledge. We further quantify how the sparsity of the communication graph affects both the optimality gap and the residual violations.
papers.reason: Decentralised voltage-constrained economic dispatch for local energy communities with learned voltage surrogate; relevant to DER and distribution-network coordination.

papers.title: The Grid's Own Language: A Common Information Model Layer for LLM Grid Assistants
papers.abstract: Assistants built on large language models (LLMs) are entering power system operation. Current designs delegate computations to validated solvers, but the agent still infers the type, role and state of each element from its name and tool-specific formats, and errors propagate to every study. The Common Information Model (CIM), the IEC standard in which operators already exchange network models, defines unambiguously what each element is and how it connects. We propose a CIM layer for LLM grid assistants and implement it in CONDUCTOR, an open-source assistant. Both the agent and its power-system studies read the layer. It labels the provenance of each fact (stated in the data, suggested only by a name, or inferred from topology), loads operators' CGMES models directly, and builds in $\leq$1\,s on the 9,241-bus PEGASE network. Deterministic checks compare every answer with solver results and the layer. On 37 tasks about the CIGRE medium-voltage and IEEE 30-bus networks, the agent gets right 97\,\% of the graded facts with the layer, such as a unit's energy source or a switch's normal state, against 55\,\% without it. We argue that a CIM layer should be a default component of grid assistants.
papers.reason: CIM information layer for LLM grid assistants in power-system operation with solver-verified answers; relevant to grid-facing agentic tools.

papers.title: AI Agents Executing an RMS and EMT Ride-Through Workflow on a 2,000-Bus Synthetic Texas Grid: A Case Study with Open-Source Tools
papers.abstract: This paper reports a case study of engineer-supervised AI agents executing a predefined RMS and EMT ride-through workflow on the 2,000-bus ACTIVSg2000 synthetic Texas grid with open-source tools. The test case is a 133 MW battery with a co-located 130 MW data-center load, assessed against ride-through criteria fixed before simulation and for loss of synchronism elsewhere in the grid. One agent ran 44 RMS cases and 15 without-project comparisons in ANDES; the other ran a 220-row EMT intake bench and an 84-row system study in DPsim and ParaEMT on a Kron-reduced area. Across the 44 RMS cases, 127 criterion cells fail, including loss of synchronism in all 44. Two findings concern the project plant. The battery keeps absorbing reactive power during sags on the light-load schedule (B3, as low as -19.8 Mvar on S4 T1), and the data-center load returns only at 5.00-5.56 s after long bolted faults (L3), which misses the ERCOT load-return requirement. In 13 of the 15 comparisons, which the authors selected after slips or speed-gate stops, the same machines slip without the project; the other 29 runs have no without-project comparison. RMS and EMT values differ in network, plant model, controls, operating point, and base, and so they are reported as separate, unaligned observations. The paper reports the errors the authors identified in the agent logs, 63 author messages, and 3.8 days from agent start to the integrated study report. The agents executed and documented the predefined ride-through and stability workflow, which covers one part of an interconnection study.
papers.reason: AI agents execute a power-grid ride-through simulation workflow with open-source tools; agentic simulation pipeline relevant to the researcher, though in power systems.

papers.title: ATLAS-Finance: Benchmarking AI Agents in Realistic Banking Environments
papers.abstract: Professional work involves under-specified assignments, where relevant information is spread across workplace applications and may conflict or change over time. To evaluate how well frontier agents can perform economically valuable work in such settings, we introduce ATLAS-Finance, a benchmark of 100 end-to-end investment-banking tasks across 13 simulated firms. As in real banking workflows, agents must search email, chat, calendars, notes, and files to identify requirements, gather information, reconcile conflicts/updates, and then build complex financial models. Tasks were developed by experienced bankers based on their real deal work and take them 15-30 hours to complete. Agent deliverables are evaluated with expert-authored rubrics (median: 124.5 criteria) covering financial rationale and results, spreadsheet construction, completeness, and formatting. Despite completing substantial portions of the requested work, current agents rarely produce correct deliverables. Across today's frontier models, the best ones (Claude Opus and Fable) pass fewer than 11% of tasks.
papers.reason: Benchmarks frontier agents on multi-step financial modelling across tool environments; relevant as an agent evaluation study, though not transport or optimisation.

papers.title: DiscoveryAgent: A Framework for Scientist-centric Agentic AI
papers.abstract: AI agents can assist scientific research, but balancing autonomous investigation with scientists' ability to inspect and redirect ongoing work remains a central design challenge. We present DiscoveryAgent, a domain-agnostic, scientist-centric system that combines autonomous investigation with scientist-directed hypothesis steering. Scientists select, refine, or replace hypotheses between research rounds, while audit agents interrogate checkpointed records to trace claims, reproduce analyses, and inform subsequent decisions. Across two predictive modeling tasks, DiscoveryAgent produced the best variable-star classifier among evaluated baselines and, with scientist steering, a protein variant-effect predictor surpassed by only one of 106 ProteinGym baselines. We develop a rigorous checkpointing system that enables highly capable audit agents, a scalable form of oversight for agentic research. Audit agents autonomously identify errors at higher rates than previous AI scientist agents, and scientists collaborating with audit agents identify 14x more valid errors versus scientists performing manual review. In three case studies led by domain experts across physical science, social science, and life science, we developed a multimodal photometric-redshift estimator that resolves complementary failures of images and photometry, achieving 0.971 AUROC for low-redshift classification; documented an 83% rise in Florida homeowners-insurance premiums from 2013 to 2023, with a growing, regressive burden; and identified CD4+ T-cell relay genes, which both receive and exert broad transcriptional regulation, enriched for autoimmune disease associations. Together, these results show how autonomous research can expand scientists' empirical reach while centering their authority over research direction and their ability to understand and challenge the evidence.
papers.reason: Scientist-steered agentic research framework with audit agents; relevant agent oversight design, though not optimisation or transport.

papers.title: GRACE: Parallel Best-of-N Multi-Agent Analysis of Closed-Form Questions over Dataframes with Guardrail Selection and Adaptive Retry
papers.abstract: LLM agents answer closed-form questions over a tabular dataframe by writing and executing Python, almost always as a single rollout: one interpretation, one script, one result, accepted without comparison. The few pipelines that produce several candidates reconcile them by answer-agreement voting, which needs a single comparable scalar and always returns one, even when every candidate is wrong. We present GRACE (Generative, Ranked, Adaptive Code Ensemble), a production-oriented pipeline that instead runs parallel best-of-N selection specialised to dataframe code. N agents run concurrently under a strict, machine-checkable output contract, diversified by persona hints, per-retry rotation, and a two-regime temperature schedule. Rather than vote, GRACE judges the executed artefacts: a pairwise tournament pre-filters the pool and a domain-specialised guardrail either selects the best candidate or, when none is defensible, rejects the whole pool and abstains with a diagnosis (an option voting structurally lacks), which in turn drives an adaptive retry with per-agent feedback. On InfiAgent-DABench (DAEval, M = 246), using Qwen3.6-35B-A3B as the backbone, GRACE raises answer match from 39% for a single-rollout baseline to 71% (+32 pp, 1.8x), recovering 53% of previously wrong answers. On the same DAEval task, the smaller dense Qwen3.5-9B lifts answer match from 38% to 63% (+25 pp, 1.7x). A controlled 3 x 3 study that sweeps the number of parallel agents against the retry budget finds, on the 35B backbone, the two levers largely substitutable: once either one is generous, the other adds little, identifying a cheap operating point for deployment. The same directional pattern replicates on the independent DataBench benchmark, again on the Qwen3.6-35B-A3B backbone, where answer match rises by 15 percentage points (from 70% to 85%) across 400 sampled questions.
papers.reason: Parallel best-of-N multi-agent code generation with guardrail selection and adaptive retry for dataframe analysis; relevant agent selection design.

papers.title: Multi-LLM Agentic AI at the Edge: Joint Agent Scheduling and Resource Allocation
papers.abstract: In this paper, an edge-enabled multi-large language model (LLM) agentic AI architecture is proposed, where one supervisor AI agent and multiple worker AI agents cooperatively execute users' requests at the edge. The supervisor AI agent decouples the user request into a series of sub-tasks and dynamically dispatches them to LLM-equipped worker AI agents via two agentic workflows, i.e., parallel and serial workflows, with a two-level retry mechanism to enhance execution reliability. To prolong the service duration of worker AI agents, the energy minimization problems are formulated by jointly considering AI agent selection and resource allocation, subject to task execution latency and quality of service (QoS) constraints. A resource allocation scheme based on alternating optimization (AO) is proposed. Specifically, for the parallel workflow, the scheme decouples the original problem into bandwidth allocation, retrieval selection and AI agent selection sub-problems, which are iteratively solved by the proposed successive convex approximation (SCA), Lagrangian relaxation (LR), and Gale-Shapley (GS) or LLM-based algorithms, respectively. For the serial workflow, the problem is similarly decoupled into service time allocation, retrieval selection and AI agent selection sub-problems; the optimal service time allocation is obtained via Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions, while the latter two sub-problems are addressed by extending the proposed algorithms to the serial scenario. Simulation results show that the proposed resource allocation scheme can reduce system energy consumption compared with other benchmarks, while experiments on a multi-LLM agentic AI system based on Qwen and Llama demonstrate improved task execution success rates.
papers.reason: Multi-LLM agent scheduling with resource allocation and optimisation (AO, SCA, Gale-Shapley) at the edge; agentic and optimisation-based but not transport-focused.

papers.title: Safely Mitigating Grid Imbalance: A Hybrid Distributional Wide-Margin Recourse Approach
papers.abstract: This paper proposes the Multi-Agent Distributional Wide-Margin Policy Gradient (MADWMPG) framework: a dual-policy hybrid imitation and safe reinforcement learning (IL-SRL) method designed for safely mitigating grid imbalance in multiphase active distribution networks with distributed soft open points (SOPs). The framework comprises a wide-margin constraint barrier recourse (WCBR) module that seeks the maximal separation of constraint-compliant and unsafe actions and learns to proactively suppress exploratory violations. The framework addresses operational volatility using a novel adaptation of noncrossing quantile regression (NQR) distributional critics that track the complete distribution of policy returns. The set of behavior and recourse policies integrates an instantaneous physics-based and differentiable action projection mechanism that generates SOP constraint-compliant actions without relying on active learning. Policy safety is made responsive using an enhancement of conventional experience replay, and the safety performance of the framework is supported by probabilistic bounds derived in the paper. The proposed framework was trained and tested on a modified multiphase IEEE 123-bus test feeder. Results demonstrate its superiority to conventional reinforcement learning and SRL methods and show that it is highly competitive against the nonlinear AC optimal power flow.
papers.reason: Safe RL for grid imbalance mitigation with soft open points in distribution networks; relevant to grid flexibility and RL for dispatch.

papers.title: Scientific Coding with Large Language Models: Evidence from Finite Element Analysis
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) offer a potential route to automating scientific programming, but their usefulness depends on consistently producing numerically correct code. We extend FEM-Bench to 17 finite element tasks involving nonlinear and history-dependent mechanics and structural dynamics, and evaluate 15 models on implementation and test generation without execution feedback. The best model succeeds in 87.1% of single-pass implementation trials, but rankings differ between tracks. The leading implementer achieves 49.9% joint test success, while the leading tester reaches 82.6%. For six models, we compare single-pass generation with two agentic harnesses that allow code execution and revision. Agentic execution solves some tasks that never succeeded in single-pass trials and improves consistency on others, but gains vary across models and harnesses, and regressions also occur. Claude Opus 5 with SimpleAgent reaches 96.5% Pass@3, the probability of at least one success in three attempts, but 77.1% Pass$^3$, the probability that all three succeed. No model-harness combination exceeds 78.8% Pass$^3$. To understand why agents submit incorrect code after passing their own checks, we analyze 249 failed agentic trajectories and identify six categories of self-verification failure. The most common are inadequate test coverage (73.1%) and reliance on generic consistency checks (70.3%), and in 28.5% of cases the tests share an error with the implementation. Motivated by these findings, an exploratory configuration with separate coder and tester agents achieves the highest observed scores, with 97.6% Pass@3 and 88.8% Pass$^3$. These results identify consistency across attempts and independent verification as the main obstacles to trusting LLM-generated scientific code.
papers.reason: Evaluates LLM agents writing and self-verifying scientific simulation code with execution feedback, relevant to agents running simulation pipelines and reliability.

papers.title: Social Welfare and Equilibrium in Distributed Microgrid Prosumer Coordination Under a Mixed Competitive-Cooperative Setting
papers.abstract: Price-based distributed prosumer coordination in distribution networks is fundamentally challenging when the aggregator pursues grid-level goals that couple prosumers' decisions, because the Lagrangian fails to separate and nodal prices are undefined under conventional dual decomposition. This paper develops a novel method that embeds mixed competitive-cooperative objectives exactly into prices, which are split into energy, congestion, and grid-objective components, closing the gap between the social welfare optimum and the competitive equilibrium. To compute the equilibrium, a distributed optimization algorithm is developed based on the projected Arrow-Hurwicz-Uzawa scheme. Explicit step-size rules are developed for the algorithm to guarantee $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{L})$ and $\mathcal{O}(1/L)$ ergodic convergence rates. Simulations on an IEEE 33-bus feeder that is connected to prosumers and electric vehicle fleets validate the accuracy and efficacy of the proposed methods.
papers.reason: Distributed prosumer coordination with EV fleets on distribution networks, with convergence guarantees; directly relevant to transport-grid integration and price-based coordination.

papers.title: Strengthening Compact Vehicle Routing Formulations through Arc-Flow Aggregation and Refinement
papers.abstract: Arc-flow formulations can provide strong relaxations for mixed-integer program formulations of vehicle routing problems, but the associated networks may be prohibitively large. We study the setting in which multiple arc flow relaxations may be applied, and introduce a dual-guided aggregation and refinement framework that constructs substantially smaller arc-flow formulations while recovering the LP bound of the original networks. Dual information is used both to identify states that can be aggregated without weakening the bound and to guide node disaggregation. We show that the resulting procedure converges finitely to the arc-flow bound of the full arc-flow formulation. The framework retains the original decision variables, allowing cutting planes to be added directly in the original variable space. Moreover, it produces an explicit MILP formulation without relying on column generation or pricing to determine the arc-flow relaxation bound. We apply our approach to the vehicle routing problem with time windows for which we define two arc flow relaxations, as well as two families of cutting planes over the original variable space. Computational experiments show that strong bounds can be obtained using substantially aggregated networks. The resulting root bounds are competitive with those obtained by the branch-and-price solver RouteOpt, while retaining a formulation that can be solved directly by a general-purpose MILP solver.
papers.reason: Arc-flow aggregation for VRPTW MILP formulations with cutting planes; strongly related to the researcher's MILP decomposition and routing interests.

papers.title: ToolGraph as a Q-Function for Test-Time Scaling of Tool-Use Agents
papers.abstract: Tool-use agents must chain interdependent calls, yet which outputs satisfy which later inputs in a deployed catalog is not something a general-purpose language model reliably infers from tool descriptions alone. We compile that structure once into a reusable external representation. ToolGraph is a directed, weighted dependency graph over a tool catalog: parameter matching and interventional probes, which execute a candidate chain with and without its proposed predecessor, propose edges whose evidence is combined into an edge confidence. Prior work uses such graphs to retrieve tools, search for tool paths, or score the next call. We ask instead whether the same structure can supply a \emph{multi-step} value by composing graph paths into a goal-conditioned action value \(Q(s,a,g)\). We study three estimators (dynamic programming over entity sets, a GraphSAGE estimator distilled from it, and an LLM scorer conditioned on graph evidence) plus a verbalizer that returns action--goal feedback to the agent, which keeps final action selection. Across two tool-use benchmarks and three backbones, we compare value ranking against personalized-PageRank retrieval over the identical graph, and against direct and reflective agents. Composition pays off only when the estimator also reads the concrete state: the LLM estimator improves on PageRank in every benchmark--backbone setting, by \(8.3\) points on average, while the two purely structural estimators fall below it, because a value defined over tool types cannot separate a correct tool called with a wrong argument. Graph construction is a one-time cost; we report it separately rather than assume it amortized away (at our scale it is comparable to request-time cost) and sweep four knobs controlling how much graph evidence to expose against success and tokens.
papers.reason: Graph-based value function for tool-use agent chaining calls; agentic planning with multi-step value, useful for agent design.

papers.title: TrainExplorer: Autonomous LLM Post-Training via Plan-and-Decouple Exploration
papers.abstract: LLM-based agents can automate model post-training, accelerating progress toward recursive self-improvement. Despite their promise, existing approaches remain under-explored and face two main challenges: (1) strategy lock-in that limits exploration beyond the initial strategy; and (2) coupled execution that obscures the effects of individual modifications. To address these challanges, we propose TrainExplorer, a multi-agent framework for autonomous post-training, that incorporates strategy planning and execution decoupling, to achieve broaden strategy exploration. First, strategy planning draws on scientific literature to construct a candidate search space of training strategies. Then, decoupled execution enables single-component interventions and attribution to guide strategy exploration. Extensive experiments on PostTrainBench demonstrate that TrainExplorer achieves a weighted aggregate score of 39.02, outperforming Claude Code using the same LLM by 7.32 and surpassing GPT-5.6 Sol-powered Codex, which scores 36.23. Code will be available.
papers.reason: Multi-agent LLM framework that plans and executes autonomous post-training experiments with decoupled attribution, akin to agents running optimisation pipelines.

papers.title: VTT: Reading Vehicle Size and Powertrain Type from Motion Trajectory Across Unseen Car Models
papers.abstract: Vehicle size and powertrain information can enrich trajectory data for traffic analysis and simulation. We present VTT, a dataset and benchmark for identifying these attributes from motion and controller area network (CAN) signals across unseen car models. The dataset contains 9,062 drives, about 3,950 h, from 1,431 vehicles and 174 car models. It provides three footprint-based size classes, powertrain labels, and evaluation on unseen car models and unseen drivers. Using 60-s windows, we compare four sequence architectures, statistical features and physical features proposed by large language models. Training with auxiliary physical targets, data augmentation and task-specific weighting raises drive-level macro-F1 to 92.6-93.0% for battery-electric versus combustion vehicles and from 62.9% to 67.1% for size classification. On public logs from 4,061 additional drivers, the full-input model identifies powertrain correctly for 86 of 88 car models; size accuracy is 63.2%, close to the internal vehicle-level result of 63.5%. Physical-feature analysis links powertrain recognition to deceleration behaviour and size recognition to steering response. Errors near size-class boundaries and limited gains from longer observations highlight the importance of label resolution and training-fleet coverage for cross-model generalisation.
papers.reason: Infers vehicle size and powertrain from CAN and trajectory data; useful for electrified fleet data and simulation inputs.

papers.title: Value and Policy Calibration from Execution Feedback for Socially Compatible Driving
papers.abstract: Autonomous vehicle (AV) decisions at intersections affect the delay, braking, and motion smoothness of surrounding human-driven vehicles (HDVs). Learning socially compatible behavior requires connecting imagined interaction outcomes with feedback from executed actions. We propose a world-model reinforcement learning framework combines imagined policy improvement with direct value and policy calibration from finalized interactions, balancing AV progress with HDV interaction burden. An interaction-aware latent model supports imagination, while off-policy correction and replay updates enable observed rewards and transitions to supervise both the critic and actor. Simulation experiments at an unsignalized intersection achieve a 100% success and reductions in following-HDV acceleration variation of 65.5% and 44.0% relative to PIWM and DreamerV3, respectively. Ablations identify complementary roles for value calibration in reducing HDV burden and policy calibration in improving passage efficiency. Tests under out-of-distribution traffic shifts further show lower ego jerk and HDV acceleration variation than PIWM at comparable passage times.
papers.reason: World-model RL for AV intersection behaviour affecting human-driven vehicles; adjacent to operations decisions but not agentic LLM or transit-specific.

papers.title: Weight-space programming for tractor guidance controller: large language models natively write neural network weights that steer a real tractor
papers.abstract: Weight-space programming is a process where a large language model reads and writes the weights of a neural network directly, guided by a natural language specification, without an optimiser or gradient descent. This study applies it to automatic tractor guidance, where a 253-parameter neural network steers along paths of lines and arcs and must be adapted when the machine changes, such as a slower steering actuator. GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 (also 5.2) edited the network for our research tractor using a small budget of simulated evaluations to repair a network trained for another tractor and write a controller into a network with zero weights. We compared them with an evolution strategy, gradient descent and pure pursuit in simulation and on the real tractor. Both models read the network and analysed the closed loop with control theory correctly, and Fable's repair without simulation succeeded only occasionally. With simulated feedback, both models repaired the trained network in single sessions and wrote a working controller from zero weights, whereas from zero the evolution strategy found none. The controllers written from zero were sparse and in a classical cascaded structure; one model edited the trained network while the other replaced it. Gradient descent reached higher accuracy with far more simulation, and all language model controllers steered the real tractor without intervention, with errors of the same order as pure pursuit. Language models can program the weights of a neural controller directly, much as control engineers design one. We call this Weight-Space Engineering.
papers.reason: LLMs directly write neural controller weights to steer a real tractor with simulation feedback, relevant to LLM-driven control design and vehicle guidance.

papers.title: A Hybrid Exact-Heuristic Solver for the Integrated Passenger and Parcel Transportation Problem
papers.abstract: We describe the solver we submitted to the second round of the SOICT 2026 contest on the Integrated Passenger and Parcel Transportation problem, a selective pickup-and-delivery routing problem with time windows, open routes and heterogeneous taxis. The solver is a single-file, standard-library Python program that combines (i) a constant-time insertion test based on latest-arrival slack, (ii) greedy insertion, local search and an Adaptive Large Neighborhood Search (ALNS) with simulated-annealing acceptance, and (iii) an exact route-selection engine that enumerates, for every taxi, the best feasible route for each request set and then solves the resulting set-packing problem by branch-and-bound strengthened with route-based large neighborhood search, Lagrangian bounds and reduced-cost fixing. The engine is chosen automatically from the instance size, and an independent verifier and a watchdog guarantee that a valid answer is always printed. On the official evaluation (38 scored instances, 5-minute limit) the solver obtained a total benefit of 487,237, finished every run within 277 s and used at most 279 MB; 28 of the 38 instances terminated well before the limit.
papers.reason: Exact-heuristic hybrid (ALNS, branch-and-bound, set packing) for a selective pickup-delivery routing problem; relevant solver methods, though not electric buses.

papers.title: A Rollout-Based Approach to Real-Time Topology and Dispatch Control in the AI4RealNet L2RPN Benchmark
papers.abstract: Operating transmission networks under uncertain outages requires coordinating discrete network topology actions with continuous adjustments to generation and storage, while respecting operational constraints and real-time computational limits. We present a rollout-based controller that combines discrete and continuous decisions under the uncertain contingency policy of the L2RPN AI4RealNet 2026 challenge. Power-flow approximations and convex optimization identify the most promising actions, followed by short-horizon simulations to predict their effect on congestion, renewable curtailment, and redispatching costs. A further policy exploits the benchmark's specific attack protocol: keeping selected lines disconnected prevents some adversarial outages from being initiated. On the benchmark's $118$-bus network, the controller completed $189$ of $208$ final-test scenarios (score $64.39$) and achieved the second-best ratio of score to computation time among the five top-ranked entries, behind one that scored lower. Our results show that combining structured optimization with simulation-based action selection is effective even without a learned decision rule, and fast enough for real-time control. Code and reproduction material: https://github.com/DavidKrame/RAD_agent__AI4RealNet_competition.
papers.reason: Rollout-based topology and dispatch control under contingencies in a power grid challenge; combines optimisation with simulation-based action selection.

papers.title: Benchmarking a Grid Foundation Model for AC Optimal Power Flow: Feasibility and Warm-Start Results on Synthetic Texas and South Carolina Grids
papers.abstract: Learning-based surrogates for alternating-current optimal power flow (AC-OPF) are often judged by the gap between their objective value and that of a nonlinear solver, which does not show that a prediction satisfies power balance and network limits. This paper tests whether predictions from the pretrained foundation model GridSFM-Open 1.1.0, recently released by Microsoft, are feasible AC-OPF operating points and whether they are useful initial values for a nonlinear solver. The model was evaluated zero-shot and after fine-tuning on 10, 100, and 1,000 labeled scenarios (FT10, FT100, and FT1000) on 500 scenarios for each of two synthetic grids, ACTIVSg2000 (Texas) and ACTIVSg500 (South Carolina), with Ipopt, MATPOWER MIPS, and pandapower PIPS as solver references. The lowest Texas median cost gap, 0.44\% for FT100, coincided with thermal violations in 24.1\% of cases and a median maximum bus power mismatch of 89 MW and 197 Mvar. Texas zero-shot predictions had a median maximum mismatch of 648 MW and 1,641 Mvar, and every South Carolina case violated a thermal limit for every model variant. Seeding Ipopt with FT1000 predictions gave geometric-mean solve-time speedups of 1.55x on South Carolina and 1.12x on Texas (p = 0.06, not significant at the 5\% level), while zero-shot seeds slowed South Carolina solves (0.26x). A small objective gap therefore did not indicate feasibility: although median zero-shot inference took only 1.32 s on Texas and 0.157 s on South Carolina on a shared host, every prediction still required a nonlinear solver, and fine-tuned predictions gave modest, grid-dependent warm-start speedups while zero-shot predictions slowed convergence on one grid. GridSFM may therefore be useful for initializing a nonlinear solver, but obtaining feasible AC-OPF solutions still required the solver.
papers.reason: Benchmarks a grid foundation model for AC-OPF warm-starts; relevant to learning-to-initialise optimisation but in power systems, not transport.

papers.title: CAE-Bench: Benchmarking AI Agents for Reusable CAE Solver Development
papers.abstract: We developed CAE-Bench, a benchmark to evaluate AI agents on Computer-Aided Engineering (CAE) solver development. A CAE solver is more than a PDE solver; it must be able to generalize across various inputs, such as different boundary conditions, geometries, and material properties. CAE-Bench evaluates the generalizability of AI-developed CAE solvers by providing the same task, such as a heat transfer problem, multiple cases, with each case specifying an input. The AI agent develops a solver for a fixed task using only a few public cases, and the resulting solver is then tested on held-out cases, i.e., cases it has never seen before. We evaluate 12 models across a range of reasoning settings on 80 computational tasks. Our experiments show that even if a solver developed by an AI agent performs well on the public cases, it may even get 0 score on held-out cases. For tasks such as fluid dynamics problems, even the solver developed by GPT-6 Astra performs poorly on held-out cases. A data format and an SDK for task registration are provided, so the researcher can use the benchmark on their own infrastructure. We hope that CAE-Bench will help the community to develop AI agents that can develop reusable CAE solvers that generalize to various inputs.
papers.reason: Benchmark for AI agents developing reusable engineering simulation solvers that generalise to held-out cases, close to agent-built simulation tools.

papers.title: Can You Undo It? Reversibility Classes for AI Agent Actions
papers.abstract: Tool-using AI agents change files, databases, access rights and public information, yet permission to call a tool does not establish whether a mistake can be undone. We present Reversibility Classes, a declared five-level vocabulary with argument-sensitive rules, conservative defaults and an explicit prior-state capture contract. The pinned implementation and evidence-linked registry cover 536 tools across 20 MCP servers. All 738 rule-case checks conform to declared expectations, while native annotation mapping differs from draft registry labels for 118 of 481 comparable tools. One AI-assisted reviewer approves 148 ratings, 75 matching the registry; this is not independent agreement. On 2,158 recorded runs, the implemented session guard gates the associated action in all 29 attributable attack-positive runs, compared with 18 for a read/write proxy, while adding nine approval points across 1,209 benign runs. Controlled file, Git, SQLite and three-browser experiments show that recovery depends on captured state, later changes, editor storage and recovery route, and expose a Git merge-state exception. The evidence supports making recovery assumptions explicit and testable. It does not establish registry-wide accuracy, reduced production harm or general recovery reliability.
papers.reason: Classifies reversibility of agent tool actions and session guards; useful for reliability of agents that make operational changes, but adjacent.

papers.title: CoopDistill: Equilibrium-Guided Multi-Agent Policy Distillation for Cooperative Driving
papers.abstract: Cooperative driving extends autonomous driving from individual vehicle decisions to joint maneuvers that improve traffic safety and efficiency. Optimization-based methods impose safety constraints but often fix paths to simplify multi-vehicle planning, limiting spatial flexibility. Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) explores alternatives through interaction, but coordinated learning and safe execution remain challenging. Their integration nevertheless faces challenges in exploration efficiency, experience allocation, and execution reliability. To address these challenges, this paper proposes CoopDistill, an equilibrium-guided multi-agent policy distillation framework. A potential-game (PG) formulation provides a fixed-path longitudinal reference, around which a residual MARL policy learns longitudinal acceleration, conflict-approach timing, and lateral path corrections. A hard-case curriculum concentrates experience on interactions that PG leaves unresolved or substantially delayed. A comparative rollout selector evaluates the joint consequences of learned corrections against PG before choosing the executed action. Experiments in merging, roundabout, and intersection scenarios compare CoopDistill with six baselines at four connected automated vehicle penetration levels. Relative to PG, success improves by 2.1--27.1 percentage points and delay decreases by 7.3--27.3\%, with no observed collisions. Code is available at https://github.com/FanGShiYuu/CoopDistill
papers.reason: Multi-agent RL with a potential-game reference for cooperative driving at merges and intersections; adjacent to traffic coordination and learned scheduling.

papers.title: Diagnosis and Recovery in AI Workflows with Scarce Expert Capacity
papers.abstract: We study sequential decisions in AI workflows and other automated execution systems where failures of uncertain origin require recovery under limited shared expert capacity. Recovery choices affect future diagnostic demand, while expert availability changes which recovery actions are worthwhile. We coordinate diagnostic requests, expert dispatch, and checkpoint-based recovery to maximize expected net operating value. A finite-horizon model tracks uncertain error locations, remaining time, and shared expert capacity. Structural analysis shows how competition for diagnosis changes unaided recovery. When a full rebuild from checkpoint 0 is the best unaided fallback after failure, a larger expert pool can justify retaining more work despite a lower chance of immediate success. Capacity can also raise net operating value before fixed staffing costs while reducing diagnostic hours when advice is requested only after a failed trial. Our Diagnosis-Resource-Recovery Control (DRRC) policy coordinates these decisions through local recovery lookahead and estimates of service requirements and remaining time; its learning-augmented variant uses task-specific quality and duration estimates. In controlled simulations, larger pools draw more requests before repair, and selective diagnosis raises net value chiefly by reducing recovery costs. In a digital twin based on 177 software defects, DRRC with reference-assisted diagnosis increases mean timely completion by 3.27 percentage points and mean net value by 1.85% relative to automated recovery, although the net-value advantage remains uncertain across repositories. Expert capacity changes when workflows seek advice and how much work they preserve. Expansion may raise or lower diagnostic hours, so capacity and recovery design should be assessed jointly by their contribution to net operating value.
papers.reason: Sequential diagnosis, expert dispatch and recovery policies for AI workflows under scarce capacity; operational decision-making close to agentic workflow optimisation.

papers.title: Discovering Programmatic Policies from Reinforcement Learning-Based Traffic Signal Controllers
papers.abstract: Traffic signal control (TSC) is critical for mitigating urban congestion. Deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has achieved strong performance by learning adaptive policies from traffic observations, but learned neural controllers are often opaque, structurally complex, and difficult to generalize across scenarios. We propose PPL-TSC, a programmatic policy learning framework that distills compact and human-readable TSC policies from DRL teachers. PPL-TSC formulates policy learning as an evolutionary search over phase utility functions (PUFs), which score candidate signal phases and select the highest-utility phase for execution. Each generation consists of four steps: policy generation, policy review, policy calibration, and policy evaluation. In the generation step, a large language model (LLM) acts as a semantics-aware evolutionary operator to propose and refine candidate PUFs. Generated PUFs are screened through explicit checks for syntactic validity, mathematical soundness, and consistency with TSC principles, with invalid ones repaired through iterative feedback. Valid PUFs are then calibrated to improve behavioral fidelity to the DRL teacher, and evaluated using a joint score combining teacher fidelity and traffic-control performance to select candidates for the next generation. Extensive experiments across diverse traffic scenarios and representative DRL-based controllers show that PPL-TSC produces compact and human-readable policies, achieves competitive performance for most teacher families, improves transfer generalization, and substantially reduces computational cost. Code is available at https://github.com/ForrestXie9/PPL-TSC.
papers.reason: LLM-driven evolutionary search for programmatic traffic signal policies distilled from DRL; relevant to LLM-designed heuristics for transport control.

papers.title: Evolving Neural Solvers for Multi-objective Combinatorial Optimization
papers.abstract: Multi-objective combinatorial optimization (MOCO) seeks high-quality solutions that represent different trade-offs among conflicting objectives. Existing neural methods typically train a dedicated model for each preference or condition a single model on different preferences. Training dedicated models becomes more costly as the number of preferences increases, while a shared model can produce duplicate solutions for different preferences, limiting the benefit of denser preference queries. We propose the Evolving Neural Solver (ENS), which trains only a small set of preference-specific models and takes advantage of evolutionary computation to evolve them into a diverse collection of solvers for better solution quality and Pareto front coverage. ENS first trains a model at an estimated knee-point preference to target a balanced compromise, then obtains the remaining initial models through parameter transfer toward the extremes, so as to preliminarily approximate the Pareto front. It then evolves these models to find more candidates that can generate non-dominated solutions through evolution strategies. Experimental results on classic MOCO problems show that ENS outperforms state-of-the-art neural MOCO methods in terms of hypervolume in most evaluated settings.
papers.reason: Neural solver for multi-objective combinatorial optimisation evolved via evolution strategies; learning-to-optimise method, not applied to scheduling.

papers.title: Exploring Low-Regret Energy System Transition Pathways with Modeling to Generate Alternatives
papers.abstract: Long-term planning of energy system transitions is complex due to interdependent investment decisions and uncertain market and policy conditions. Stochastic optimization models account for this uncertainty by identifying a single optimal hedging strategy. However, the flexibility in technology choice and investment timing, i.e., the transition flexibility, usually remains unexplored. Modeling to generate alternatives (MGA) explores near-optimal solution spaces but has not been coupled with stochastic optimization to quantify the transition flexibility. We explore the low-regret pathway space, i.e., all transition pathways that stay within a chosen regret tolerance in every scenario. We introduce a termination criterion for MGA that bounds the exploration error in high-dimensional solution spaces and measure how far each pathway decision, once taken, narrows the capacity ranges of the others. We apply the method to an industrial energy system in Germany. The pathway that minimizes the worst-case regret keeps it at 2.2%, compared with up to 30.9% for perfect-foresight pathways. The transition flexibility increases most at low regret tolerances. At 3.5%, the capacity ranges are on average about 60% as wide as at the highest regret tolerance of 10%. A large share of these capacity ranges is surplus capacity, i.e., capacity installed in addition to, not instead of, other capacity. Surplus capacity is largely not operated but, once installed, narrows the other capacity ranges more strongly than operated capacity. Exploring the low-regret pathway space, rather than reporting a single optimal pathway, therefore is the more informative basis for planning energy system transitions under uncertainty.
papers.reason: Modeling to generate alternatives combined with stochastic optimisation for low-regret energy transition pathways; useful optimisation methodology background.

papers.title: GainCtrl: Predicting Remaining Gains for Efficient LLM Agent Execution
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used to power agents that interact with tools and environments to solve complex tasks. Repeated attempts improve the quality of tool-using agents, but continued execution incurs additional costs even when it is unlikely to improve the best result ultimately returned. This raises the question of when to stop an attempt to reduce execution cost while preserving task-level Best-of-N quality. To address this question, we introduce GainCtrl, a gain-based execution controller for LLMs. In GainCtrl, a lightweight CPU predictor uses interaction histories to estimate expected positive gains over retained scores, which are then used to guide stopping decisions with calibrated thresholds to limit the loss in mean Best-of-N task quality. We evaluate the controller through trajectory replay across three environments and three LLM actors. Comparisons of interpolated quality-cost Pareto frontiers show that GainCtrl generally uses fewer tokens than baselines at matched target quality. Fixed policies also achieve quality close to that of full execution while substantially reducing token consumption. The predictor runs at millisecond latency on a single CPU thread, supporting repeated monitoring without access to LLM internals.
papers.reason: Predicts when to stop LLM agent executions to save cost, a budgeted operational decision relevant to agent workflow efficiency.

papers.title: GranularGPT: Natural-Language-Driven End-to-End Discrete Element Method Simulations
papers.abstract: Discrete element method (DEM) simulations are widely used to investigate granular and particulate systems, but their application often requires specialized expertise in particle physics, numerical modelling, and simulation post-processing. Large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities to simplify these workflows by enabling users to interact with simulation tools through natural language. This study offers GranularGPT, an LLM-assisted agentic framework for end-to-end DEM simulation workflows, from natural-language problem descriptions to simulation execution and automated post-processing. The framework enables users to generate DEM simulation cases, execute and monitor simulations, and automatically extract and report physical and process-level metrics. Evaluation across 60 normal-condition cases covering 12 DEM scenarios and parameter variations achieve a simulation success rate of 91.7%. In the error-handling evaluation, all 10 repairable errors are detected and 9 are successfully resolved, while all 5 non-repairable cases are correctly identified and reported. The framework automatically extracts a range of DEM-relevant metrics, including particle size distributions, packing and density measures, velocity profiles, discharge rates, mixing indices, contact force characteristics, and thermal quantities. GranularGPT provides a foundation for improving the accessibility and efficiency of DEM simulation workflows while reducing the specialized expertise required for their operation.
papers.reason: LLM agentic framework that runs end-to-end DEM simulations from natural language, closely matching LLM-driven simulation pipelines though not transport.

papers.title: Learning to Clear Peer-to-Peer Energy Markets
papers.abstract: Peer-to-peer energy markets are a promising paradigm for integrating distributed energy resources. A large body of work models their clearing as distributed optimization or generalized Nash equilibrium (GNE) problems which let prosumers coordinate trades and local resources without a central operator. Yet, the computational and communication burden of distributed optimization and GNE-seeking algorithms poses a major challenge to deployment at scale. We propose a learning-to-optimize framework for decentralized markets that uses historical data to accelerate clearing algorithms without additional communication. To enforce convergence by design, we train summable augmentations to a baseline algorithm, using graph neural networks to learn permutation-equivariant updates for markets of varying size and topology. We instantiate the framework for computing a variational GNE in the market model of Le Cadre et al. (2020) with a distributed Douglas-Rachford algorithm, but the idea extends to other models and base algorithms. Numerical experiments show improved convergence and illustrate the robustness of our method to out-of-distribution instances.
papers.reason: Learning-to-optimise with GNN-augmented distributed algorithms for peer-to-peer energy market clearing; relevant ML-for-optimisation method in energy systems.

papers.title: PISG: Constraint-Aligned Signal Amplification for Diffusion-Based Combinatorial Optimization
papers.abstract: Diffusion-based solvers have become a prominent approach to neural combinatorial optimization. At inference time, they assign each decision variable a prediction score. A greedy decoder ranks candidates by these scores and checks hard constraints to ensure feasibility. Top-ranked candidates should be both promising and jointly feasible, making prediction-constraint alignment critical. When this alignment is weak, greedy decoding skips constraint-violating candidates and falls back to lower-ranked alternatives, degrading solution quality. Existing test-time methods improve search, sampling, or decoding, but do not directly strengthen this alignment before decoding. We observe that trained denoisers already carry constraint-aligned structural signals. Building on this observation, we propose Perturbed Instance-Structure Guidance (PISG), a training-free method that amplifies these signals at test time. At each denoising step, PISG constructs a structure-degraded prediction and extrapolates the unperturbed prediction away from it. The resulting guided prediction improves candidate rankings before constrained decoding. Signal analysis shows that this guidance concentrates on constraint-critical variables rather than uniformly rescaling scores. Under greedy decoding and without downstream refinement, PISG improves all 16 TSP solver-scale pairs across DIFUSCO, T2T, FastT2T, and StruDiCO, and all four MIS-ER solvers, with MIS-ER solved-cost gains up to +4.8%. The gains persist on most large-scale settings after 2-opt, and a preliminary study extends PISG to a Transformer-based solver. These results identify prediction-constraint alignment as an effective test-time enhancement direction for diffusion-based combinatorial optimization. Code is available at https://github.com/Ming-321/PISG.
papers.reason: Training-free test-time guidance for diffusion neural combinatorial solvers on TSP and MIS; relevant learned optimisation method.

papers.title: Routing Beyond Task Categories: A Cost-Aware LAB-Bench Study
papers.abstract: We tested whether features of biology questions or of a model's first answer can improve accuracy within an inference budget. In a LAB-Bench pilot, we compared a category router with one that adds six structural features. Neither reached the primary 80% accuracy target on development. At the 50% and 60% secondary targets, both chose Haiku for all 120 held-out questions and scored 71/120. We then froze a new comparison before collecting responses on 144 additional questions. Semantic routing scored 86/144. A policy that could defer after reading Haiku's answer scored 87/144. Both stayed within the inference budget of USD 0.678 per 1,000 queries. Against a 95% Haiku and 5% GPT mixture, the accuracy gains were 0.66 percentage points for semantic routing and 1.35 points for deferral. The paired 95% intervals were [-0.28,2.25] and [-0.14,3.47] points. A simple rule that escalated Haiku nonanswers scored 92/144 at USD 0.710 per 1,000 queries, above the budget. A retrospective nonanswer rule with a calibration-selected escalation probability gave an expected 85.63/144. At the learned deferral policy's observed inference cost, post hoc interpolation gave an expected 86.14/144. In a later development check, Astra and Gemini each scored 30/40. The best tested policy in each router family matched that score. The pair covered 33/40 in hindsight. The routers missed the 32/40 criterion, so the proposed 120-question evaluation did not start.
papers.reason: Cost-aware routing among LLMs under an inference budget with deferral policies; agent decision-making under budget constraints is adjacent to the researcher's interests.

papers.title: Sage S2.1 Flash Technical Report
papers.abstract: We introduce Sage S1.5 Flash, a 320-billion-parameter general-purpose mixture-of-experts model designed to reason over scientific evidence and act in interactive environments. Sage Sci-Perception uses dedicated encoders for molecular graphs and biological sequences and represents spectra as ordered patches of measurements. Modality-specific projectors map these representations into the input space of a shared backbone, which processes them alongside text and images. To develop the model's agent capabilities, we construct verifiable environments for tool use, search, and coding, as well as specialized workflows involving machine learning experiments and scientific software. Task completion is checked against execution results, changes in environment state, or submitted artifacts. We evaluate Sage S1.5 Flash on 33 benchmarks across seven domains. In the primary comparison against five baselines, it ranks first on OfficeQA Pro (72.2), MLE-bench Lite (90.3 HumanRank), Harvey LAB, and SpreadsheetBench~2, and second on OSWorld-Verified (85.2), WebArena-Verified (67.6), and DeepResearch Bench~II (54.2). These results show particular strengths in using documentary evidence, producing verifiable workbooks, and carrying out machine learning tasks, alongside competitive performance in desktop and browser workflows that require the model to act on visual feedback.
papers.reason: General agentic model tech report with tool use and ML experiment workflows; relevant agentic AI context but not optimisation-focused.

papers.title: Slower but Faster: When Self-Organized Traffic Flows Beat Traffic Signal Control
papers.abstract: Urban traffic flow networks are complex adaptive systems, whose variability challenges centralized, top-down control. We study decentralized alternatives in which order emerges from local interactions, comparing the network-wide performance of roundabouts in SUMO against fixed-time and actuated control as well as self-organizing signals on a 4$\times$4 grid and a rewired, irregular variant of it, across demand levels and periodic surge amplitudes. In our computer simulations of the regular grid, converting the single most central intersection already lowers delays by 2 to 3\% relative to actuated control; each additional conversion lowers them further, and full conversion outperforms every signalized alternative under all conditions studied. In the irregular traffic flow network with full conversion of all intersections into roundabouts, this holds only up to a critical load, where traffic flow breaks down sharply, when the time-averaged demand reaches about 3.1 times the base load. Beyond that point, the self-organizing traffic signals show the lowest delay of any network-wide strategy and is nearly insensitive to surges. Interestingly, roundabouts are favorable solutions even at lower speed limits: in the regular grid, compared to the mean speed under actuated control at a speed limit of 50\,km/h, roundabouts match that speed at a speed limit of about 40\,km/h. Compared to traffic signal control, this establishes a slower-is-faster effect. Furthermore, travel times in self-organized traffic flows are more predictable than in networks with conventional signals.
papers.reason: SUMO comparison of roundabouts, signals and self-organizing control; relevant simulation of urban traffic networks but not electrified bus operations.

papers.title: System 1 agents: a method for local, reliable and fast agentic AI
papers.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence could automate analyses of sensitive clinical data, but current agents depend on large language models (LLMs). Cloud LLMs expose patient data. Local LLMs hallucinate, and an invented value in a tool call propagates through every later step. Here we present a method to build System 1 agents: local agents that call tools without generating text. A deterministic compiler turns each tool's schema and the request into multiple-choice questions whose options come from the request and the schema, then a one-pass decision model answers them. On 1,952 requests to 157 biomedical tools, the best System 1 agent chose the right tool, or correctly declined, for 97.0% of requests, significantly ahead of all 18 local LLM-agent settings (best 95.2%). The System 1 agent filled 97.0% of 6,056 stated argument values. No System 1 call contained invented content, against 5.5-19.7% of LLM calls. The System 1 Agents framework is freely available as open-source software at https://github.com/eltzanis/SystemOneAgents.
papers.reason: Local deterministic tool-calling agents avoiding LLM text generation; reliable agent design relevant to operational agents, though clinical focus.

papers.title: Tie-Line Scheduling Using Real-Time Contraction Metrics: Hierarchical Reachable Sets for Multi-Area Inverter-Dominated Grids
papers.abstract: Managing transmission congestion in multi-area power grids dominated by inverter-based resources (IBRs) requires bridging a severe timescale and modeling divide. Supervisory congestion optimizers -- such as Online Feedback Optimization (OFO) and two-tiered differentiable Model Predictive Control (MPC) -- rely on linearized, convex algebraic grid approximations that cannot guarantee dynamic stability during sub-second converter transients. Conversely, fast distributed consensus schemes like Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) depend on convex plant assumptions and iterative message exchanges that lag behind rapid tie-line surges. This paper replaces convex ADMM emergency consensus with a Distributed Nonlinear Separable Control Contraction Metric (SCCM) architecture spanning three nested tiers: the Device layer, the Area layer, and the Grid tie-line layer. By pairing online Prediction Error Method and Moving Horizon Estimation (PEM-MHE) parameter tracking with offline convex Linear Matrix Inequality (LMI) synthesis, the controller executes a closed-form nonlinear feedback law online without solving real-time optimization problems. We derive the Pontryagin attainable (reachable) ellipsoids for each layer, prove hierarchical tube containment via Schur-complement matrix inequalities, and project the certified Grid reachable tube through Power Transfer Distribution Factors (PTDFs) to supply guaranteed safe thermal limits to the supervisory coordinator. Validation on modified IEEE 39-bus (100% IBR, zero synchronous generators) and 3-area IEEE 118-bus systems demonstrates an 82.8% reduction in cumulative tie-line thermal overload while maintaining strict exponential contraction ($λ_{\max} \le -2.43$) even under a 3 s communication blackout.
papers.reason: Hierarchical contraction-based tie-line control for IBR-dominated grids; relevant to transport-grid integration only at the power-system level.

papers.title: Turing Agent: Agentic Formal Verification for Mathematical Research
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly advancing mathematical discovery, moving beyond benchmark-level problem solving to tackle frontier research problems. This progress is ushering mathematics into an era of proof abundance, raising a fundamental challenge: how can we ensure the correctness of the ever-growing volume of AI-generated proofs and transform them into trustworthy, machine-verified mathematical knowledge? We introduce Turing Agent, an agent harness designed to orchestrate end-to-end formal verification of research-level mathematics. Its wo-scale architecture integrates theorem formalization and proof formalization agents, empowered by structured proof decomposition, parallel verification, accumulated proof experience, and selective semantic review. Leveraging our collaborations with theoretical computer science (TCS) researchers, we focus our evaluation on TCS, a particularly demanding domain characterized by intricate quantification, complex dependencies, and stringent semantic requirements. Against direct generation and general-purpose coding harnesses, including Codex CLI and Claude Code, Turing Agent achieves approximately 57-62% faithful formalization success on Formal TCS Bench and 83% overall pass@1 on a TCS-focused subset of RLMEval, using GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro. Notably, Turing Agent, built on DeepSeek, successfully completes the formal verification of three previously unresolved TCS tasks from OpenAI's October 2026 collection. One particularly challenging TCS problem required about a hundred formally verified auxiliary claims. Moreover, by actively exploring and refining the formalization process, Turing Agent can uncover simpler alternative proofs, expose unnecessary dependencies in original proofs, and generate reusable mathematical knowledge as a byproduct of verification.
papers.reason: Agent harness orchestrating formal verification of research mathematics with parallel agents; agentic workflow for scientific tasks, not transport.

papers.title: WeVisForensics: Self-Evolving Agent for Omni AI-Generated Video Detection
papers.abstract: Recent advances in video generation call for reliable detection grounded in explicit forensic evidence. However, current methods primarily depend on single-pass chain-of-thought reasoning that overlooks brief or localized artifacts, or on predefined multi-agent workflows that offer limited flexibility in selecting relevant inspections. Even with adaptive investigation, optimizing the investigation policy alone does not directly improve the forensic capabilities of fixed experts. We introduce WeVisForensics, an agentic framework in which a main investigator agent coordinates a self-evolving library of forensic inspector sub-agents spanning visual and audio cues. The investigator learns which artifact type to examine, over which window, and when to conclude, and these interactions provide shared feedback for both levels of agents. Our dual-timescale policy optimization strategy, DTPO, closes this loop through fast reinforcement learning of the investigator and slower refinement of the inspectors, guided by annotated artifact intervals, to report subtle artifacts they once dismissed. Furthermore, we curate ForenCue-30K, combining role-specific forensic annotations and interaction trajectories to supervise individual inspections and their coordination, with an accompanying reinforcement-learning pool. Experiments show that WeVisForensics averages 95.2% detection accuracy across in-domain, out-of-domain and agentic benchmarks, 9.0% above the strongest prior detector, while grounding its verdicts in localized evidence.
papers.reason: Agentic video forensics framework with self-evolving sub-agents and RL policy optimisation; agentic planning is relevant but the application is far from transport.
